cost: A new freeway now costs well over a billion dollars. The LBJ Express cost $2.6 billion for 13 miles of I-635, about $200 million a mile.

The region's long-range plan, Mobility 2050, puts $97.5 billion into roads and $57.9 billion into rail and bus through 2050. Its authors say that eliminating the worst congestion would take road spending four to five times the size of the entire plan.
household: Households pay too. Owning and running a new car costs about $12,900 a year, and DFW households spend 18.6% of their budget on getting around, more than the national average.
The average DFW commuter lost 69 hours to traffic delay in 2024, and 849 people died on the region's roads.
people: And roads only serve people who can drive. A quarter of the region's residents are under 18. One in eight is 65 or older, and by 85 four in ten have given up their license. One in ten adults rarely or never drive.
One in fifteen Dallas County households has no car at all; in the City of Dallas it was one in ten.
budget: That is not a radical number. Mobility 2050 already plans about $57.9 billion for rail and bus over 25 years, beside $97.5 billion for roads, though that figure most likely also pays to run and maintain today's systems, while this plan's {budget_b} a year is for building alone (running the new lines costs about {opex_2050} a year by 2050, {opex_per_res} per resident). The difference is that this plan keeps going, every year, on a network designed around where people live and work.
peers: Other American regions already spend this much. Seattle's Sound Transit 3 spends about $630 per resident a year and LA's Measure M about $310. This plan is about {per_res} per resident today.
Texas cities are building too: Houston's METRONext and Austin's Project Connect were approved by voters.
appetite: When Texans vote on transit, they mostly say yes: Houston (68% in 2019), San Antonio (68% in 2020) and Austin (58% in 2020).

The support isn't unanimous. In May 2026 three DART member cities voted on leaving: Addison (70%) and University Park (54%) stayed, Highland Park left. In NCTCOG's 2024 survey for Mobility 2050, 48% of respondents named expanding transit the region's biggest challenge.
People already ride where service is good: DART's light rail carries about 65,000 trips on an average weekday, and the Silver Line opened in October 2025.
